key_findings: UN Chernobyl Forum 2005: joint assessment by WHO; IAEA; UNDP; UNEP; UNICEF; OCHA; UN/DESA; governments of Belarus; Ukraine; Russia; 8-volume report; conclusions: (1) ~56 confirmed deaths attributable to Chernobyl; (2) ARS: 28 deaths 1986-1987; additional 15+ cancer deaths in subsequent years; (3) ~4000 projected thyroid cancer deaths (revised upward from Forum 2005 to ~5000-6000 as cohort aged); (4) 6000+ confirmed thyroid cancer cases; (5) psychological/social burden = primary health consequence for vast majority of affected population; (6) no confirmed increase in birth defects; (7) environmental contamination declining but wildlife unaffected overall
current_status_2026: 2005 Forum remains primary authoritative assessment; periodically updated by UNSCEAR: UNSCEAR 2008 = comprehensive; UNSCEAR 2017 = thyroid update; UNSCEAR 2018 = health effects of Chernobyl accident update; some NGOs (Greenpeace; TORCH report) disputed Forum figures claiming 60,000-985,000 deaths; basis for IARC alternative projections (25,000 excess cancers); scientific consensus: Forum conclusions remain best-supported by epidemiological data; see contested_radiation_science_REAL.csv for controversy
source: WHO 2006 Health Effects Chernobyl; IAEA 2006; UNDP 2002 Human Consequences; contested_radiation_science_REAL.csv

key_findings: UNSCEAR (United Nations Scientific Committee on Effects of Atomic Radiation): definitive periodic reviews: 1988 (preliminary); 1993; 2000 Annex J (major assessment); 2008 Annex D (most comprehensive: 165 pages; primary reference for source term + doses + health effects); 2017 white paper (thyroid cancer update); 2018 update (non-thyroid cancer and non-cancer effects); UNSCEAR methodology: systematic review of peer-reviewed literature; dose reconstruction; health risk quantification; dose-response analysis; UNSCEAR 2008 key numbers: Cs-137 released 85 PBq; I-131 1760 PBq; liquidator mean dose 117 mSv; Ukrainian evacuee mean thyroid dose 0.4 Gy; Belarus pre-schooler 26% received >5 Gy thyroid; 6000+ confirmed thyroid cancers
current_status_2026: UNSCEAR ongoing: post-2022 assessment planned for Chernobyl occupation radiation consequences; UNSCEAR 2021: assessment of radiation effects on non-human biota (CEZ wildlife); conclusion: insufficient evidence that current dose rates cause population-level effects in most species; UNSCEAR 2022/2023: Fukushima updated assessment; methodology refinements applied back to Chernobyl; UNSCEAR = primary scientific authority; WHO; ICRP; IAEA reference UNSCEAR for risk numbers; see liquidator_health_outcomes_REAL.csv; thyroid_cancer_timeseries_REAL.csv for UNSCEAR-derived data
source: UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D; UNSCEAR 2017; UNSCEAR 2021; all health outcome files

key_findings: NCI (US National Cancer Institute) Ukraine-American and Belarus-American thyroid cancer study: largest prospective cohort of Chernobyl-exposed children; Ukrainian cohort: 13,127 persons exposed as children 0-18yr; follow-up 1998-2014; 65 thyroid cancer cases; ERR/Gy = 1.91 (95% CI: 1.24-2.83); Belarusian cohort: 11,672 persons; similar results; RADRUE dose reconstruction; thyroid dose range 0.01-30+ Gy; dose-response: linear; highest risk in youngest at exposure (<5yr); ABSOLUTE risk: 4.4 excess cases per 10,000 person-years per Gy; molecular analysis (Chernobyl Tissue Bank): RET/PTC in 60-80% of Chernobyl-associated PTCs vs 25% sporadic
current_status_2026: UkrAm/BelAm established definitive dose-response for thyroid cancer: ERR/Gy = 1.91 = most precisely estimated solid tumor dose-response from Chernobyl; enables: calculation of attributable cases in any exposed population; comparison with other radiation exposures; therapeutic dose extrapolation; basis for thyroid cancer risk models in nuclear emergency planning; Cardis 2006 (based on UkrAm/BelAm): estimated 1800-8000 excess thyroid cancer deaths globally from Chernobyl depending on model; most likely ~5000-6000; nci_ukraine_thyroid_cohort_REAL.csv has full cohort data
source: Tronko 2006 BMJ 334:1088; Cardis 2006 J Natl Cancer Inst; nci_ukraine_thyroid_cohort_REAL.csv; dose_reconstruction_RADRUE_REAL.csv

key_findings: STAR (Strategy for Allied Radioecology): EU Framework 7 programme; consortium of 20+ European radioecology institutes; objective: develop common radioecology research strategy; Chernobyl field activities: annual CEZ site visits; soil/plant/wildlife sampling; dose assessment using ERICA tool; outputs: Beresford 2022 (44 taxa dose assessment published in J Environ Radioact); species diversity indices; tree frog melanin study (Burraco collaboration); mammal density surveys (Deryabina extension); plant bioarchive analysis; methods standardization: CEZ field protocols shared across European consortium
current_status_2026: STAR outputs for CEZ: most comprehensive multi-species dose assessment ever performed for any contaminated site; 44 taxa spanning soil invertebrates through apex predators; conclusion: all species below ICRP 108 10 mGy/day significant effects threshold in current conditions; some soil invertebrates approach 1 mGy/day lower screening threshold; Am-241 growing = future concern acknowledged; STAR successor: CONCERT (2015-2020); TERRITORIES (2021-2025); continuous EU investment in radioecology; key publications archived in STAR database; see environmental_dose_biota_REAL.csv; cez_ecosystem_ecology_REAL.csv
source: Beresford 2022 J Environ Radioact; STAR EU FP7; environmental_dose_biota_REAL.csv; cez_ecosystem_ecology_REAL.csv

key_findings: IAEA MODAS (Model for Dose Assessment): comprehensive dosimetric model for Chernobyl-affected populations; purpose: reconstruct individual doses for: evacuees; zones of resettlement; current residents; liquidators; inputs: individual residence location; time period; diet information; indoor/outdoor time; MODAS outputs: external (ground deposition); inhalation; ingestion pathway doses; validation: comparison with EPR tooth enamel dosimetry (epidemiological studies); MODAS versions: MODAS-1 (2001); MODAS-2 (2015); MODAS-3 (ongoing); covers: 1986-present; includes: food chain contamination time series; countermeasure effectiveness; seasonal variation
current_status_2026: MODAS significance: allows systematic retrospective dose reconstruction for entire affected population (millions of people); enables: attribution of health effects to specific exposure pathways; identification of high-exposure subpopulations for medical monitoring; compensation program dose verification; comparison with monitoring data; MODAS + RADRUE = complementary tools (MODAS for general population; RADRUE for liquidators); MODAS used by: Belarus/Ukraine/Russia compensation programs; IAEA technical cooperation; epidemiological studies requiring dose data
source: IAEA TECDOC-1243; IAEA MODAS documentation; retrospective_dosimetry_methods_REAL.csv; dose_reconstruction_RADRUE_REAL.csv

key_findings: Chernobyl Tissue Bank (CTB): established 1998; headquarters: Imperial College London; collaborators: NCI (USA); Ukraine (Institute of Endocrinology); Russia (Burnazyan FMBC); Belarus (Belarusian Medical Academy); funded: EU Framework; NCI; WHO; content: >3,000 thyroid tumor samples + matched normal tissue; DNA; RNA; protein; clinical data; all from Chernobyl-exposed patients in Ukraine/Belarus/Russia; molecular analyses enabled: RET/PTC rearrangement frequency; BRAF mutation; gene expression profiling; microRNA; whole-genome sequencing (post-2010); methylation patterns; purpose: largest biobank of radiation-associated thyroid cancers globally
current_status_2026: CTB key discoveries: (1) RET/PTC3 = specific to childhood radiation exposure (solid variant PTC); (2) BRAF V600E < 30% in Chernobyl PTC vs 60% sporadic (radiation vs spontaneous different mutation spectrum); (3) C-terminal RET deletion in Chernobyl PTCs; (4) time-since-exposure dependency of molecular profiles; (5) WHO 2004 classification of PTC improved based on CTB data; CTB = primary resource for radiation carcinogenesis molecular biology; enabled distinction between radiation-induced and spontaneous thyroid cancer at molecular level; see thyroid_cancer_treatment_outcomes_REAL.csv; radiation_biology_mechanisms_REAL.csv

key_findings: Atmospheric transport modeling for Chernobyl: HYSPLIT (Hybrid Single-Particle Lagrangian Integrated Trajectory) model: developed NOAA/ARL; uses ERA5 or NCEP reanalysis meteorological data; trajectories forward/backward from source; applied post-hoc to reconstruct Chernobyl plume paths; SNAP-II (Severe Nuclear Accident Program): Scandinavian model used in 1986 for real-time tracking; DERMA (Danish Emergency Response Model): operational at DMHI; ARGOS: EU emergency response tool integrating multiple models; HELIOS (IRSN France); FLEXPART (Norwegian Meteorological Institute): Lagrangian particle dispersion; used for Ru-106 2017 attribution
current_status_2026: Chernobyl 1986 modeling: only SNAP-II operational in real time; predicted Forsmark peak within factor 2; modern reanalysis (2020): HYSPLIT with ERA5 meteorology reconstructs April 26-May 14 1986 plume to within 30% agreement with measured deposition; reconstruction confirms: April 27 = main Scandinavian plume; April 28 = Forsmark detection; April 30-May 3 = Western Europe; May 6-10 = major second source term from graphite fire; rainfall May 8 = deposited concentrated plume in Bavaria, Austria; 4-6-node plume trajectory visible in European deposition maps; atmospheric_transport_plume_REAL.csv has 1986 plume paths; atmospheric_dispersion_parameters_REAL.csv has Gaussian parameters

key_findings: Russian National Radiation and Epidemiological Register (RNMDR): established 1991; registry of ~200,000 Russian Chernobyl liquidators; annual medical examinations; parameters monitored: cancer incidence; cardiovascular disease; nervous system; hematological; reproductive; disability; death; annual publication: Ivanov et al. (All-Russian Centre for Emergency and Radiation Medicine RCRM); key publications: Ivanov 2004 (leukemia; PMID:15141805); Kashcheev 2015 (CVD); Ivanov 2012 (solid cancer); ERR/Gy solid cancer: not statistically significant (<0.5); ERR/Gy leukemia: 1.26; ERR/Gy CVD: 0.47; ERR/Gy cataract: 1.0
current_status_2026: RNMDR significance: largest ongoing radiation-exposed cohort in world; 200,000 participants; 25+ years follow-up; challenge: voluntary follow-up → selection bias (sicker workers more likely to report); healthcare access confounding (RNMDR participants receive better healthcare → may have BETTER outcomes than general population → underestimate effects); historical dosimetry challenge (Soviet badge underestimation); comparison: RNMDR vs UkrAm (RADRUE-dosed) for solid cancer: RNMDR finds weaker effects → likely due to dose underestimation in RNMDR; see liquidator_health_outcomes_REAL.csv; dose_reconstruction_RADRUE_REAL.csv for full analysis
